question: Why are Southeast claims taking longer to close since May 2026?

report.interpretation: Cycle time is the agreed metric: the median days from report date to close date for closed claims, grouped by report month. I looked at Southeast (FL, GA, NC) claims reported from May 2026 and compared them with January–April 2026. I left out August and September 2026 from the comparison because those months are still incomplete.
report.answer: The slowdown is real, and it lines up with two Southeast adjusters leaving. The median cycle time for Southeast claims rose from about 28 days (Jan–Apr reports) to about 38 days (May–Jul reports). It peaked at 40 days for July reports. ADJ-016 left on 2026-05-01 and ADJ-017 left on 2026-05-15, and no one replaced them in the data. The region went from 6 adjusters to 4, so each handles about 25–27 new claims a month instead of about 16. Cycle time rose across nearly every cause of loss, which fits a capacity problem. Texas, California and North did not show a comparable rise. The apparent improvement for Aug–Sep reports isn't real. Those claims are mostly still open, so only the quick ones count as closed.
report.answer_sql: SELECT strftime(report_date,'%Y-%m') AS report_month, count(*) AS claims, count(distinct adjuster_id) AS adjusters, round(count(*)*1.0/count(distinct adjuster_id),1) AS claims_per_adjuster, median(close_date-report_date) FILTER (WHERE status='closed') AS median_days_to_close FROM claims WHERE region='Southeast' AND report_date>=DATE '2026-01-01' AND report_date<DATE '2026-08-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

findings.claim: Southeast median cycle time rose from the Jan–Apr level to May–Jul, while other regions stayed roughly flat.
findings.evidence_sql: SELECT region, CASE WHEN report_date>=DATE '2026-05-01' THEN 'post' ELSE 'pre' END AS per, median(close_date-report_date) AS med, count(*) AS n FROM claims WHERE report_date>=DATE '2026-01-01' AND report_date<DATE '2026-08-01' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1,2

findings.claim: Two Southeast adjusters left in May 2026 (ADJ-016 on May 1, ADJ-017 on May 15). The four remaining adjusters (ADJ-018 to ADJ-021) absorbed their claims, so the caseload per adjuster rose by about 60%. Each of the four now takes longer to close claims than before.
findings.evidence_sql: SELECT c.adjuster_id, a.leave_date, CASE WHEN report_date>=DATE '2026-05-01' THEN 'post' ELSE 'pre' END AS per, count(*) AS n, median(close_date-report_date) AS med FROM claims c LEFT JOIN adjusters a USING(adjuster_id) WHERE c.region='Southeast' AND report_date>=DATE '2026-01-01' AND report_date<DATE '2026-08-01' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY per, n DESC

key_numbers.label: Claims per adjuster per month, Jan–Apr
Claims per adjuster per month, May–Jul

findings.claim: The slowdown is broad. Collision rose from 23 to 31 days, water damage from 37 to 54, theft from 31 to 43 and glass from 6 to 10.5. Repair shops don't explain it, because both preferred and non-preferred shops slowed (preferred 20 to 27 days, non-preferred 15.5 to 25).
findings.evidence_sql: SELECT CASE WHEN report_date>=DATE '2026-05-01' THEN 'post' ELSE 'pre' END AS per, cause, count(*) AS n, median(close_date-report_date) AS med FROM claims WHERE region='Southeast' AND report_date>=DATE '2026-01-01' AND report_date<DATE '2026-08-01' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY cause, per

hypotheses.hypothesis: Adjuster attrition and a higher caseload per adjuster
hypotheses.evidence: Two of six Southeast adjusters left in May, and the load per adjuster rose from about 16 to about 26 claims a month. The timing matches the slowdown. This is a correlation: the data can't prove the departures caused it.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A particular repair shop or network status
hypotheses.evidence: Preferred and non-preferred shops both slowed by about 7–10 days.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A shift in the mix of causes toward slower claim types
hypotheses.evidence: Most causes slowed individually. The share of slow bodily injury and liability claims did not rise (30 of 315 claims after, 33 of 379 before).

The May–Jul figures are mostly complete, with 5–20 claims per month still open, so they slightly understate the true slowdown. Aug–Sep figures are distorted because their slowest claims are still open. There were no duplicate rows.
Median cycle times in the other regions stayed within a few days of their earlier levels.

data_quality_issues.issue: Cycle time counts only closed claims, and recent report months have many claims still open (62 open for Aug and 114 for Sep in the Southeast).
data_quality_issues.impact: Aug–Sep cycle times (28 and 9 days) look faster than they will end up. Don't read them as a recovery.

data_quality_issues.issue: Report volume in the Southeast rose in Aug–Sep (143 and 135 claims, against about 100 a month before).
data_quality_issues.impact: Caseload per adjuster is even higher in those months. I didn't investigate the cause, and it may add to the backlog.

proposed_actions.reason: Four adjusters are carrying the work of six. Their open backlog is growing (114 September-reported claims still open), and report volume is rising.

open_questions: Was a replacement hire planned for the Southeast, and have the departed adjusters' claims been reassigned evenly?
What is behind the jump in Southeast claim reports in Aug–Sep 2026?

tool_calls.sql:
WITH source AS (
    SELECT c.*, p.channel, p.metro,
           coalesce(pay.paid, 0) AS paid_to_date,
           coalesce(pay.paid, 0) + c.reserve_amount AS incurred,
           c.close_date - c.report_date AS days_to_close
    FROM claims c
    JOIN policies p USING (policy_id)
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT claim_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM claim_payments GROUP BY claim_id
    ) pay USING (claim_id)
)
SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', report_date) AS DATE) AS period, region, median(days_to_close) FILTER (WHERE status = 'closed') AS value
FROM source
WHERE report_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND report_date <= DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY ALL
